title: The Heisenberg Uncertainty Principle
lead: Because a particle is also a wave, where it will be found can only be given as a probability. The idea runs from electrons arriving one by one at a screen to Heisenberg's limit on how well the position and the momentum of a particle can be known together, a limit a wave packet makes visible.
objectives: To understand that sometime you cannot know everything about a quantum system as demonstrated by the Heisenberg uncertainly principle.
notes: Adapted from OpenStax College Physics and the LibreTexts uncertainty-principle module under CC BY 4.0. The embedded YouTube video on wave packets and the slit experiment is left out; the wave-packet figure carries its idea.

Exercise 3 is printed twice in the book, as Exercise 9.11.1 and Exercise 19.E.1, on two pages that carry the uncertainty-principle text of Quantum States of Atoms and Molecules; its solution is AI-written. Numeric answers accept a 2% tolerance.

figures.original_caption: The building up of the diffraction pattern of electrons scattered from a crystal surface. Each electron arrives at a definite location, which cannot be precisely predicted. The overall distribution shown at the bottom can be predicted as the diffraction of waves having the de Broglie wavelength of the electrons (CC BY 4.0; OpenStax).

The animation shows the relevant spreads in the uncertainty for position and momentum of light/photons (light wave's corresponding photon particle). From the result of de Broglie, we know that for a particle with known momentum, p will have a precise value for its de Broglie wavelength can be determined (and hence a specific color of the light).

exercises.prompt: What is the maximum uncertainty of velocity the electron described in Example 1.9.1 ?

answer.hint: Equation 1.9.5 is an inequality: which way does it bound $\Delta v$?
answer.solution: Infinity. There is no limit in the maximum uncertainty, just the minimum uncertainty.

exercises.prompt: Estimate the minimum uncertainty in the speed of an electron confined to a hydrogen atom within a diameter of $1 \times 10^{-10} m$?

answer.hint: The uncertainty in position is half the diameter; then $\Delta v \ge \hbar/(2 m \Delta x)$.
answer.solution:
We need to quantify the uncertainty of the electron in position. We can estimate that as $\pm 5 \times 10^{-10} m$. Hence, substituting the relavant numbers into Equation 1.9.5 and solving for $\Delta v$ we get

$$ \Delta v= 1.15 \times 10^6\, km/s $$

Notice that the uncertainty is significantly greater for the electron in a hydrogen atom than in the magnesium atom (Example 1.9.1) as expected since the magnesium atom is appreciably bigger.

exercises.prompt: Compare the minimum uncertainty in the positions of a baseball (mass = 140 gm) and an electron, each with a speed of 91.3 miles per hour, which is characteristic of a reasonable fastball, if the standard deviation in the measurement of the speed is 0.1 mile per hour. Also compare the wavelengths associated with these two particles. Identify the insights that you gain from these comparisons.

parts.hint: Convert both speeds to m/s, take $\Delta p = m\Delta v$, and use Equation 1.9.5 for $\Delta x$ and $\lambda = h/mv$ for the wavelength.

answer.solution:
In SI units the speed is 91.3 mi/h = 40.8 m/s and its standard deviation is 0.1 mi/h = 0.0447 m/s. The uncertainty in momentum is $\kdp = \km\kdv$, and Equation 1.9.5 puts the smallest $\kdx$ at $\hbar/(2\kdp)$.

$$ \kdx_{\text{ball}} \ge \dfrac{1.055\times10^{-34}\ \text{J s}}{2(0.140\ \text{kg})(0.0447\ \text{m/s})} = 8.4\times10^{-33}\ \text{m} $$ $$ \kdx_{e} \ge \dfrac{1.055\times10^{-34}\ \text{J s}}{2(9.109\times10^{-31}\ \text{kg})(0.0447\ \text{m/s})} = 1.3\times10^{-3}\ \text{m} $$

The de Broglie wavelength is $\klambda = h/\km v$:

$$ \klambda_{\text{ball}} = \dfrac{6.626\times10^{-34}\ \text{J s}}{(0.140\ \text{kg})(40.8\ \text{m/s})} = 1.2\times10^{-34}\ \text{m} $$ $$ \klambda_{e} = \dfrac{6.626\times10^{-34}\ \text{J s}}{(9.109\times10^{-31}\ \text{kg})(40.8\ \text{m/s})} = 1.8\times10^{-5}\ \text{m} $$

The baseball's two lengths are $10^{17}$ to $10^{19}$ times smaller than a proton, far below anything a measurement can reach, so its position and path are as sharp as classical mechanics says. An electron moving at the same speed, measured as well, cannot be placed better than to about a millimetre, and its wavelength is 18 μm. Both lengths go as $1/\km$, so they differ by the mass ratio, about $1.5 \times 10^{29}$. The uncertainty and the wave nature of matter show only when the mass is very small.

footnotes.html: The momentum of a photon is not its frequency: it is $h/\lambda$, which equals $h\nu/c$, so it is proportional to the frequency.
Figure 1.9.2 is a wave packet; the patterns built up by single particles are those of Figure 1.9.1, and the double slit is the experiment of Section 1.7.
Half of a diameter of $1 \times 10^{-10}$ m is $\pm 5 \times 10^{-11}$ m, not $\pm 5 \times 10^{-10}$ m; the speed below is the one this smaller value gives.
The unit is m/s: $\hbar/(2 m_e \Delta x) = 1.0546\times10^{-34}/(2 \times 9.109\times10^{-31} \times 5\times10^{-11}) = 1.16 \times 10^{6}$ m/s.
